¶
'''throttle-damper''' (throt′l-dam″pėr), ''n.'' An adjustable damper.

'''throttle-lever''' (throt′l-lev″ėr), ''n.'' In steam-engines, the hand-lever by which the throttle-valve is worked: used chiefly in locomotive engines. See cut under ''passenger-engine.''

'''throttler''' (throt′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''throttle'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who or that which throttles or chokes.

'''throttle-valve''' (throt′l-valv), ''n.'' A valve in the steam-pipe of a boiler for controlling the flow of steam to any apparatus, more particularly such a valve placed in the eduction-pipe of a steam-engine.

'''through'''<sup>1</sup> (thrö), ''prep.'' and ''adv.'' [Also sometimes ''thro, thro'''; < ME. *''thrugh, thruch, thruc, thruh'' (= OFries. ''thruch''), a transposed form of ''thurgh, thurh'', etc., < AS. ''thurh'', through: see ''thorough'', which is the reg. mod. form of the word, now partly differentiated, being used chiefly as an adj., while ''through'' is used as the prep. and (less exclusively) as the adv. Nearly all the ME. instances belong to ''thorough.'' Cf. ''thrill''<sup>1</sup> for ''thirl''<sup>1</sup>, ult. from ''through, thorough.''] I. ''prep.'' 1. From one side or end to the other side or end of; from the beginning to the end of: expressing transition or motion from or as from one point to another. {{smaller|Specifically — (''a'') Denoting passage from one point to another, especially in a direct line from one end or side to the other end or side of something, either by penetration or by motion in and along some passage, opening, or space already formed: as, to bore a hole ''through'' a beam; to pass ''through'' a town;}}

This is one of few bird-names of wide native range in the Indo-Eur. languages. (''g'') Cf. OBulg. ''drozgŭ'', Russ. ''drozdŭ'', a thrush. (''h'') Cf. F. ''trâle'', a throstle; from Teut.] 1. A thrush; especially, the song-thrush or mavis, ''Turdus musicus''. See ''thrasher''2, and cut under ''thrush''1. [British.] {{smaller block|The ''throstel'' old, the frosty feldefare. {{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 364.}} I herde the jaye, and the ''throstelle'', The mawys menyde of hir songe. {{right|''Thomas of Ersseldoune'' (Child's Ballads, I. 98).}} The ''throstle'' with his note so true, The wren with little quill. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 1. 130.}} In the gloamin o' the wood The ''throssil'' whusslit sweet. {{right|''Motherwell'', Jeanie Morrison.}}}} 2. A machine for spinning wool, cotton, etc., from the rove, consisting of a set of drawing-rollers with bobbins and fliers, and differing from the mule in having the twisting-apparatus stationary, and also in that it twists and winds simultaneously and continuously. {{smaller|Yarn from the throstle is smooth, and is used for sewing-thread and the warp of heavy goods, while yarn from the mule is soft and downy, and is used for the weft of heavy goods, and both warp and weft of light goods. Also called ''water-frame'', because at first driven by water, and originating in the water-frame of Arkwright. See cut under ''water-frame''. Also ''throstle-frame''.}} {{smaller block|Yarn, as delivered from the mule in woollen-spinning, or from the ''throstle'' in the case of worsteds, is in the condition known as singles. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIV. 659.}}}} '''throstle-cock''' (thros′l-kok), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''thrustle-cock'', ''thresel-cock''; < ME. ''throstelcok'', ''throstelkok'', ''throstylkock'', ''thrustelcok'', ''threstelcok'', ''thyrstyllecok''; < ''throstle'' + ''cock''1. Cf. ''thricecock''.] The male mistlethrush. [Prov. Eng.] {{smaller block|The ousel and the ''throstle-cocke'', Chief musick of our Maye. {{right|''Drayton'', Shepherd's Garland. (''Nares''.)}} Methinks I hear the ''thresel-cock'', Methinks I hear the jaye. {{right|''Little Musgrave and Lady Barnard'' (Child's Ballads, II. 18).}}}} '''throstle-frame''' (thros′l-frām), ''n.'' Same as ''throstle'', 2. '''throstling''' (thros′ling), ''n.'' [Appar. < ''throstle'' + ''-ing''1, after ''thrush''2 confused with ''thrush''1 (?).] A disease of cattle occasioned by a swelling under the throat. '''throttle''' (throt′l), ''n.'' [< ME. *''throtel'' = G. ''drossel'', the throat; dim. of ''throat''.] 1. The throat. {{smaller|(''a'') The gullet or swallow: same as ''throat'', 2 (''a'').}} {{smaller block|Leaving all claretless the unmoistened ''throttle''. {{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, xiv. 58.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') The windpipe or thropple: same as ''throat'', 2 (''b'').}} {{smaller block|Æneas with that vision stricken down, Well nere bestraught, vpstart his heare for dread, Amid his ''throatel'' his voice likewise 'gan stick. {{right|''Surrey'', Æneid, iv. 361.}} At the upper extream it [the bittern] hath no fit larinx or ''throttle'' to quallifie the sound, and at the other end by two branches deriveth itself into the lungs. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., iii. 27.}}}} 2. A throttle-valve. {{smaller block|If the engine is not fitted with driver-brakes, he must}} reverse the engine and again open the ''throttle''. {{right|''Scribner's Mag.'', VI. 332.}} '''throttle''' (throt′l), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''throttled'', ppr. ''throttling''. [< ME. ''throtlen'' (= G. ''er-drosseln''); < ''throttle'', ''n''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To choke; suffocate; have the throat obstructed so as to be in danger of suffocation. ''Imp. Dict.''—'''2.''' To breathe hard, as when nearly suffocated. ''Imp. Dict.'' '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To choke; suffocate; stop the breath of by compressing the throat; strangle. {{smaller block|'Tis but to pull the pillow from his head,
And he is ''throttled''. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, ii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|They seized him, pulled him down, and would probably soon have ''throttled'' him. {{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, xxxiii.}}}} '''2'''†. To pronounce with a choking voice; utter with breaks and interruptions, like a person half suffocated. {{smaller block|I have seen them shiver and look pale,
Make periods in the midst of sentences,
''Throttle'' their practised accent in their fears. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., v. 1. 97.}}}} '''3.''' To obstruct by a throttle-valve or otherwise: said of steam, a steam-pipe, or a steam-engine. {{smaller block|When the ports and passages offer much resistance, the steam is expressively said to be ''throttled'' or wire-drawn. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXII. 487.}}}} {{smaller block|The engine was running nearly at full power, very slightly ''throttled''. {{right|''The Engineer'', LXV. 430.}}}} ='''Syn.''' '''1.''' ''Strangle'', etc. See ''smother''. '''throttle-damper''' (throt′l-dam″pėr), ''n.'' An adjustable damper. '''throttle-lever''' (throt′l-lev″ėr), ''n.'' In steam-engines, the hand-lever by which the throttle-valve is worked: used chiefly in locomotive engines. See cut under ''passenger-engine.'' '''throttler''' (throt′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''throttle'' + ''-er''1.] One who or that which throttles or chokes. '''throttle-valve''' (throt′l-valv), ''n.'' A valve in the steam-pipe of a boiler for controlling the flow of steam to any apparatus, more particularly such a valve placed in the eduction-pipe of a steam-engine. '''through'''1 (thrö), ''prep.'' and ''adv.'' [Also sometimes ''thro, thro'''; < ME. *''thrugh, thruch, thruc, thruh'' (= OFries. ''thruch''), a transposed form of ''thurgh, thurh'', etc., < AS. ''thurh'', through: see ''thorough'', which is the reg. mod. form of the word, now partly differentiated, being used chiefly as an adj., while ''through'' is used as the prep. and (less exclusively) as the adv. Nearly all the ME. instances belong to ''thorough.'' Cf. ''thrill''1 for ''thirl''1, ult. from ''through, thorough.''] I. ''prep.'' 1. From one side or end to the other side or end of; from the beginning to the end of: expressing transition or motion from or as from one point to another. {{smaller|Specifically — (''a'') Denoting passage from one point to another, especially in a direct line from one end or side to the other end or side of something, either by penetration or by motion in and along some passage, opening, or space already formed: as, to bore a hole ''through'' a beam; to pass ''through'' a town;}} to creep ''through'' a hole; to march ''through'' the streets; to see ''through'' a telescope; to cut ''through'' several thicknesses; to pass ''through'' a doorway. Sometimes emphatically reduplicated, as in the phrase ''through and through.'' {{smaller block|Thy slander hath gone ''through and through'' her heart. {{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 1. 68.}}}} {{smaller block|I'd make this ten mile forty mile about, Before I'd ride ''through'' any market-town. {{right|''Middleton (and others)'', The Widow, iii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Oftentimes they vse for swords the horne of a Deere put ''through'' a peece of wood in forme of a Pickaxe. {{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, I. 132.}}}} {{smaller block|The Court could not see . . . that the nation had outgrown its old institutions, . . . was pressing against them, and would soon burst ''through'' them. {{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}} {{smaller block|If we look ''through'' a pane of red glass, rays which come ''through'' it to the eye from a white object will be red. {{right|''Amer. Jour. Psychol.'', II. 638.}}}} (''b'') From the beginning to the end of; in or during the course of; coincident with: as, to enjoy good health all ''through'' life. {{smaller block|They alledge the antiquity of Episcopacy ''through'' all Ages. {{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}} {{smaller block|A shapeless mound, cumbrous with its very strength, and overgrown, ''through'' long years of peace and neglect, with grass and alien weeds. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 22.}}}} (''c'') Throughout; over the whole surface or extent of; in all directions in; all over: as, to travel ''through'' the country. {{smaller block|In the same Prouince of Tanguth is Succuir, whose Mountaines are clothed with Rheubarbe, from whence it is by Merchants conueyed ''through'' the World. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 427.}}}} {{smaller block|By us, your Fame shall ''thro''' the World be blaz'd. {{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Ovid's Art of Love.}} Mental emotions undoubtedly destroy life by the overwhelming perturbation which they produce ''through'' the whole nervous system. {{right|''J. M. Carnochan'', Operative Surgery, p. 98.}}}} {{smaller block|(''d'') Expressing passage in and out of, among, along, or within some yielding medium, or separable or penetrable aggregate: as, to move ''through'' the water, as a fish or a ship; to wander ''through'' the jungle; to run the fingers ''through'' the hair.}} {{smaller block|Afore I will endure such another half day with him, I'll be drawn with a good gib-cat ''through'' the great pond at home. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Bartholomew Fair, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|We glide serenely enough ''through'' still deep reaches where the current is insignificant. {{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XLIII. 629.}}}} {{smaller block|(''e'') Expressing complete passage from one step to another in any series or course of action or treatment: as, to go ''through'' an operation; to go ''through'' college (that is, a course of instruction in college); to go ''through'' a course of treatment or training.}} '''2.''' Among: expressing a succession of experiences in passing along any course to ultimate exit or emergence: as, to pass ''through'' perils or tribulations. {{smaller block|And I must blame all you that may advise him;
That, having help'd him ''through'' all martial dangers,
You let him stick at the kind rites of peace. {{right|''Chapman'', Byron's Conspiracy, iv. 1.}}}} '''3.''' By way of: expressing a preliminary or intermediate stage. {{smaller block|The brown plain far and wide
Changed year by year ''through'' green to hoary gold. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 201.}}}} '''4.''' By means of: expressing instrumentality, means, or agency. {{smaller block|It is ''through'' me they have got this corner of the Court to cozen in. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Mercury Vindicated.}} All salvation is ''through'' Christ. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, i. 54.}}}} ¶ 5. By reason of; on account of; in consequence of; out of: expressing reason or actuating principle or impulse: as, to run away ''through'' fear. {{smaller block|He rested him on the floore, unfitte ''through'' his rusticity for a better place. {{right|''Spenser'', To Sir Walter Raleigh.}}}} {{smaller block|This proceedes ''through'' the barbarous ignoraunce of the time, and pride of many Gentlemen. {{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|I feel my fault, which only was committed ''Through'' my dear love to you. {{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Cannot you surmise the weakness which I hitherto, ''through'' shame, have concealed even from you? {{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Himself secure in the wise liberality of the successive administrations ''through'' which he had held office, he had been the safety of his subordinates in many an hour of danger and heartquake. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 12.}}}} '''To break, get, go, look,''' etc., '''through.''' See the verbs. '''II.''' ''adv.'' 1. From one end or side to the other: as, to pierce or bore a thing ''through.'' See ''thorough, adv.'' {{smaller block|Truth has rough flavours if we bite it ''through.'' {{right|''George Eliot'', Armgart, ii.}}}} 2. From beginning to end: as, to read a letter ''through.''—3. To the end; to the ultimate purpose: as, to carry a project ''through.''—4. To the end or terminal point, as of a line of travel: as, that ticket will take you ''through.''—5†. Thoroughly. {{smaller block|I protest Myself ''through'' rarified, and turned all flame In your affection. {{right|''B. Jonson,'' Sejanus, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller|'''Through and through,''' thoroughly; out and out: as, a method ''through and through'' speculative.—'''To bear, carry, fall, put,''' etc., '''through.''' See the verbs.—'''To be through,''' to have finished; have done: as, ''are'' you ''through?'' [Colloq.]—'''To drop through,''' to fall to pieces; come to naught; fail or perish: same as ''to fall through:'' as, the scheme ''dropped through.''}} {{smaller block|Through idleness . . . the house ''droppeth through.'' {{right|Eccl. x. 18.}}}} '''through'''1 (thrö), ''a.'' [< ''through''1, ''adv.'' Cf. ''thorough, a.''] 1. Clear; open; unobstructed. {{smaller block|Was there not a ''through'' way then made by the swoord for the imposing of lawes uppon them? {{right|''Spenser,'' State of Ireland.}}}} 2. That extends or goes with little or no interruption or without change from one important or distant place to another: as, a ''through'' line of railway; a ''through'' train; a ''through'' passenger.—3. That entitles to transportation to the end of the line or succession of lines by which some distant point is reached: as, a ''through'' ticket; a ''through'' bill of lading.—{{smaller|'''Through bolt,''' a bolt which passes through from side to side of what it fastens.—'''Through bridge.''' See ''bridge.''—'''Through coal,''' the name given in the South Wales coal-field to a mixture of large and small coal. Also called ''altogether coal,'' and in Somersetshire ''brush-coal.'' None of these terms are used in the United States.—'''Through fang.''' See ''fang.''—'''Through rate,''' a rate or price charged for carrying goods or passengers to a distant destination, over the routes of various}} carrying companies, as by rail, steamer, coach, etc., generally fixed at a lower figure than the consignor or passenger could obtain by separate arrangement with each company.—'''Through ticket,''' a railway- or steamboat-ticket good for the whole of a journey, often entitling the holder to travel on the lines or conveyances of more than one company.—'''Through traffic,''' the traffic from end to end of a railway system, or between two important centers at a wide distance from each other: opposed to ''local traffic.''—'''Through train''' a train which goes the whole length of a long railway route; a train running between two or more important centers at long distances, especially when it makes few or no stoppages by the way.
